text: {"master_id": "pat-martino", "work_id": "linear-expressions", "usage_notes": [{"chord_quality": "m7", "function_role": "minor-tonic-activity-anchor", "narrative": "For minor seventh chords, Martino prescribes identifying the chord's inversion form (1-4) and selecting the corresponding numbered activity: Form 1 maps to Activities 1 and 5, Form 2 to Activity 2, Form 3 to Activity 3, Form 4 to Activity 4. The chord inversion is the operative selector -- melodic choice follows from it rather than from independent judgment. Chapter 1, p. 10.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:chord-activity-mapping/chord-inversion-selects-activity"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 1 p.10"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "m7", "function_role": "positional-key-assignment", "narrative": "For minor seventh chords, Martino prescribes determining the key not from the chord name alone but from the position on the neck where the activity form is played: the same activity shape in third position is G minor, in fifth position is A minor, etc. Position is the key selector; the form is key-neutral. Chapter 1, p. 11.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:chord-activity-mapping/position-determines-key"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 1 p.11"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "m7", "function_role": "cyclic-octave-wraparound", "narrative": "For minor seventh chords encountered after completing all five activity forms, Martino prescribes cycling back to Activity 1 one octave higher rather than stopping -- Activities 1 and 5 share the same chord inversion (Form 1) and the same sixth-string starting note (G), making the system infinitely repeatable up the neck. Chapter 1, p. 15.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:chord-activity-mapping/cyclic-octave-wraparound"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 1 p.15"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "m7", "function_role": "horizontal-transposition-prerequisite", "narrative": "For minor seventh chords, Martino prescribes mastering all five activity forms horizontally in all twelve keys before advancing to Phase II (vertical movement). The Phase I completion rule is explicit and non-negotiable: 'Then and only then should you move onto PHASE II.' Chapter 1, p. 16.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:chord-activity-mapping/position-determines-key"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 1 p.16"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "maj7", "function_role": "relative-minor-reduction", "narrative": "For major seventh chords, Martino prescribes substituting the relative minor seventh: Cmaj7 = Am9 (relative minor). This reduction allows the player to apply the minor-based activities system directly to major seventh chords without learning a separate vocabulary. Chapter 3, p. 50.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/relative-minor-reduction"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 3 p.50"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj9", "function_role": "secondary-relative-minor-reduction", "narrative": "For major ninth chords, Martino prescribes optionally substituting the secondary relative minor (III chord of the major key): Cmaj9 = Em7. This provides a second substitution path when the primary relative minor (Am7) is harmonically less desirable. Chapter 3, p. 50.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/secondary-relative-minor-fallback"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 3 p.50"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj6", "function_role": "relative-minor-reduction", "narrative": "For major sixth chords, Martino prescribes substituting the relative minor seventh: Cmaj6 = Am7. The major sixth and its relative minor share all pitch content; the substitution is direct and requires no additional voice-leading adjustment. Chapter 3, p. 50.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/relative-minor-reduction"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 3 p.50"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7", "function_role": "minor-via-perfect-fifth-reduction", "narrative": "For dominant seventh / ninth chords (treated as quality-equivalent: C7 = C9 = C13), Martino prescribes converting to a minor form rooted a perfect fifth above the dominant root -- e.g., G9 -> Dm6 (up a P5). This closes the three-way substitution loop among m7b5, m6, and dominant ninth. Chapter 4, p. 55.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/dominant-ninth-perfect-fifth-up-rule", "pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/same-quality-interchange"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.55"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7alt", "function_role": "step-up-minor-substitution", "narrative": "For altered dominant chords, Martino prescribes moving up one half-step from the dominant root and playing minor -- e.g., for Gb7 altered, play G minor. This single interval-direction instruction replaces the altered chord with a minor form the activities system can handle directly. Chapter 4, p. 57.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/altered-dominant-step-up-minor-rule"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.57"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "dom7alt", "function_role": "scale-choice-over-altered-dominant", "narrative": "For altered dominant chords, Martino prescribes melodic minor over harmonic minor as the scale of choice because only melodic minor contains the b7 -- the 'hot' note of the dominant seventh chord. Harmonic minor supplies b9, #9, b5, and #5 but omits the b7, making it insufficient for fully expressing the altered dominant sound. Chapter 4, p. 57.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/melodic-minor-preference-over-altered-dominant"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.57"}], "provenance": "extracted", "cross_ref": ["dom7alt/harmonic-minor-proscription"]}, {"chord_quality": "dom7alt", "function_role": "harmonic-minor-avoided-over-altered-dominant", "narrative": "Do not substitute harmonic minor over an altered dominant as a first-choice scale: although harmonic minor yields the altered 9ths and 5ths (b9, #9, b5, #5), it lacks the b7, which is the defining tone of a dominant seventh chord. Harmonic minor is a weaker choice; melodic minor is prescribed instead. Chapter 4, p. 57.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/melodic-minor-preference-over-altered-dominant"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.57"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive", "cross_ref": ["dom7alt/scale-choice-over-altered-dominant"]}, {"chord_quality": "m7b5", "function_role": "minor-via-minor-third-substitution", "narrative": "For half-diminished (m7b5) chords, Martino prescribes moving up a minor third from the m7b5 root and playing minor -- e.g., Bm7b5 -> Dm6 (up a m3). The rationale is explicit: m7b5 is an incomplete dominant ninth chord and is inversionally equivalent to m6 in third inversion, making the substitution harmonically coherent rather than approximate. Chapter 4, p. 55.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/m7b5-minor-third-up-rule"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.55"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "m7b5", "function_role": "inversion-equivalence-with-m6", "narrative": "For half-diminished chords, Martino prescribes understanding their inversional equivalence to m6: Bm7b5 is Dm6 in third inversion; conversely, Dm6 is Bm7b5 in first inversion. This bi-directional equivalence is the conceptual foundation for the m7b5-to-minor substitution rule and explains why the same activities apply across both chord types. Chapter 4, p. 55.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/m7b5-minor-third-up-rule"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.55"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "aug", "function_role": "minor-maj7-via-major-sixth-substitution", "narrative": "For augmented triads, Martino prescribes going up a major sixth from the root and playing melodic or harmonic minor (preferring melodic minor). Because every augmented triad has three enharmonic root names, three distinct minor-maj7 substitutions are available from a single chord -- e.g., F augmented yields Dm(maj7), F#m(maj7), and Bbm(maj7). Martino provides a diagram showing each enharmonic root name and its corresponding minor-maj7 target. Chapter 4, p. 56.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/augmented-triad-major-sixth-up-rule"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.56"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "aug", "function_role": "enharmonic-root-tripling", "narrative": "For augmented triads, Martino prescribes treating each of the triad's three notes as a valid root name -- the triad inverts to form two other augmented triads enharmonically, so F aug = A aug = Db aug. This tripling of available root names is the prerequisite step before applying the major-sixth-up minor-maj7 substitution rule. Chapter 4, p. 55.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/augmented-triad-major-sixth-up-rule"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.55"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj", "function_role": "slash-chord-relative-minor-substitution", "narrative": "For major triads appearing as slash chords (major triad over a bass note), Martino prescribes converting the major triad to its relative minor and reinterpreting the bass note as a scale degree of that minor key. For example, C/F# becomes Am with the F# treated as the 6th of A minor. Chapter 4, p. 56.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/relative-minor-reduction"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.56"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "maj", "function_role": "slash-chord-secondary-relative-minor-fallback", "narrative": "For major triad slash chords where the primary relative minor clashes with the bass note (e.g., creating a b5 in the bass), Martino prescribes falling back to the secondary relative minor -- the III chord of the major key. For Db/E, Bb minor is rejected because E creates a b5 against it; F minor (III of Db major) is prescribed instead. The F harmonic minor scale is validated by containing all pitch content of the slash chord. Chapter 4, p. 56.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/secondary-relative-minor-fallback"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.56"}], "provenance": "extracted", "cross_ref": ["maj/slash-chord-relative-minor-proscription"]}, {"chord_quality": "maj", "function_role": "slash-chord-b5-bass-clash-avoidance", "narrative": "Do not apply the primary relative minor substitution to a major triad slash chord when the bass note creates a b5 against the substitute minor root -- this interval clash is explicitly cited as the disqualifying condition that forces the secondary relative minor fallback. Chapter 4, p. 56.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/secondary-relative-minor-fallback"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.56"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive", "cross_ref": ["maj/slash-chord-secondary-relative-minor-fallback"]}, {"chord_quality": "m6", "function_role": "inversion-equivalence-with-m7b5", "narrative": "For minor sixth chords, Martino prescribes understanding their inversional equivalence to m7b5: Dm6 is Bm7b5 in first inversion. The equivalence table in Chapter 3 also shows Cm7b5 = Ebm6, making m6 and m7b5 freely interchangeable within the substitution system. Chapter 3, p. 50; Chapter 4, p. 55.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/m7b5-minor-third-up-rule"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 3 p.50"}, {"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.55"}], "provenance": "extracted"}, {"chord_quality": "m6", "function_role": "dominant-ninth-substitution-target", "narrative": "For minor sixth chords as substitution targets, Martino prescribes using them as the output form of the dominant-ninth reduction: G9 resolves to Dm6 (minor rooted a perfect fifth above G). The m6 form is the preferred minor target -- not plain m7 -- when reducing a dominant ninth. Chapter 4, p. 55.", "source_principle_ids": ["pat-martino:linear-expressions:harmonic-substitution-reduction/dominant-ninth-perfect-fifth-up-rule"], "source_work_id": "linear-expressions", "references": [{"source": "linear-expressions", "citation": "chapter 4 p.55"}], "provenance": "extracted"}]}
